For here, as in many other places, whatever profit is collected returns entirely to the King. Bordering this place are the workshops of the goldsmiths, whose consul <note>leader of the guild</note> keeps the seal and the dies for the coins. In Fez <note>original: "Fessa"</note>, neither a ring nor anything else can be manufactured from gold or silver unless the metal has first been sealed: for they punish transgressors most severely. However, once the metal is sealed, whatever is made from it is weighed as if it were currency. The greatest part of the goldsmiths who inhabit New Fez consists of Jews, and they carry and sell gold and silver vessels to Old Fez at a certain place situated not far from the spice merchants. For in Old Fez, neither gold nor silver is struck, nor are Muslims <note>original: "Mahumetani"</note> permitted to practice that art, because they would be considered usurers <note>fœneratores</note> if they were to resell any silver or gold work for more than its proportionate weight, although this is granted to the Jews by the governors of the city. You may also find some here who only manufacture vessels for the citizens, to whom wages are paid only in proportion to their labor. That part of the city which the Royal Guards formerly inhabited

<summary>This page describes the minting and goldsmithing regulations in Fez, noting the strict control over precious metals and the role of the Jewish community in the jewelry trade. It highlights the religious restrictions preventing Muslims from certain metalworking practices due to laws against usury.</summary>
